title.en: History: Early Revolts against British Rule in Tamil Nadu

text.en: Raju saw a statue of a brave Tamil fighter. "Did the south revolt against the British?" he asked.

Before 1857, Tamil Nadu saw early revolts against the British East India Company. Pulithevar of Nerkattumseval fought against the Company's tax claims. Veerapandiya Kattabomman of Panchalankurichi refused to pay tax and was hanged in 1799.
Marudhu Brothers of Sivaganga led a revolt and issued the Tiruchirappalli Proclamation calling for unity against the British. Dheeran Chinnamalai of Kongu country fought with the support of Tipu Sultan's methods.
The Vellore Revolt of 1806 was a rising of Indian soldiers against changes in dress that hurt their religious feelings. Though crushed, these revolts showed early resistance.
Before 1857, Tamil Nadu saw early revolts against the British East India Company.
Pulithevar of Nerkattumseval fought against the Company's tax claims.
Veerapandiya Kattabomman of Panchalankurichi refused to pay tax and was hanged in 1799.
Marudhu Brothers of Sivaganga led a revolt and issued the Tiruchirappalli Proclamation calling for unity against the British.
Dheeran Chinnamalai of Kongu country fought with the support of Tipu Sultan's methods.
The Vellore Revolt of 1806 was a rising of Indian soldiers against changes in dress that hurt their religious feelings.
Though crushed, these revolts showed early resistance.
Long before 1857, local Tamil chieftains—called Palayakkarars or Poligars—resisted when the Nawab of Arcot handed tax-collection rights to the British East India Company.
Originally created under the Vijayanagara and Madurai Nayak rulers, 72 Palayams governed fortified territories across Tirunelveli and Madurai.
Between 1755 and 1767, Pulithevar of Nerkattumseval became India's first local ruler to openly defeat a British Company force near Vasudevanallur.
Notice another remarkable hero: Ondiveeran, a valiant commander in Pulithevar's army who struck British camps in daring night raids.
In Sivaganga, Queen Velu Nachiyar—aided by loyal brothers and minister Thandavarayan Pillai plus Hyder Ali—reclaimed her kingdom in 1780, becoming India's first queen to defeat the British.
During that fortress battle, warrior Kuyili coated herself in oil and set ablaze the British gunpowder storehouse to open the gates for Velu Nachiyar's troops.
Later in Panchalankurichi (Thoothukudi district), young Palayakkarar Veerapandiya Kattabomman boldly questioned British tribute collector Colin Jackson at Ramanathapuram.
After Bannerman besieged Panchalankurichi fort with heavy cannon in 1799, Kattabomman escaped briefly but was captured and calmly walked to the gallows at Kayathar on 16 October 1799.
Soon after, his brother Oomathurai joined the Marudhu Pandiyar brothers—Periya Marudhu and Chinna Marudhu—of Sivaganga to unite South Indian rebels.
In June 1801, the Marudhu Brothers issued the historic Tiruchirappalli Proclamation pasted on Srirangam temple walls—urging Indians of every caste and religion to expel the foreigners.
Though thousands fought bravely in the 1800–1801 South Indian Rebellion, British cannons took Kalaiyarkoil and hanged hundreds, razing Panchalankurichi to the ground.
Meanwhile in Kongu Nadu (Erode–Salem belt), Dheeran Chinnamalai refused Nawab and British taxes, trained an army with Tipu Sultan's French instructors, and won victories at Cauvery and Odanilai.

board.text: Dheeran Chinnamalai wins 3 battles in Kongu

text.en: Betrayed by his cook Nallappan, Dheeran Chinnamalai too was hanged at Sankagiri Fort in July 1805.
Then on 10 July 1806 came the dramatic Vellore Revolt inside Vellore Fort—fifty-one years before Meerut 1857!
Tipu Sultan's sons were housed inside Vellore Fort while Indian sepoys boiled over harsh British pay cuts and Commander Agnew's new leather-cockade turban regulations.
Hindus feared losing caste marks and Muslims feared shaving beards; at 2 a.m. on 10 July 1806 sepoys seized the fort and raised Tipu's tiger flag.

board.text: Sepoys hoist Tipu's flag over Vellore Fort

text.en: Colonel Gillespie rushed cavalry from Arcot with cannons, brutally crushing the rising, yet the British dropped the hated uniform order afterward.

board.text: Revolt crushed, but Agnew turban scrapped

text.en: Even though British divide-and-rule and modern artillery defeated each rising one by one, the memory stayed alive in Tamil folk ballads.

board.text: Why early revolts failed militarily yet inspired

text.en: Compare northern & southern milestones: Bengal had Plassey (1757), while Pulithevar (1755), Velu Nachiyar (1780) and Vellore (1806) proved Tamil resistance started first.
Remember hero–place pairs cleanly: Pulithevar–Nerkattumseval, Velu Nachiyar–Sivaganga, Kattabomman–Panchalankurichi, Chinnamalai–Odanilai/Sankagiri.
Notice the 1801 Carnatic Treaty: Britain dismantled Palayakkarar forts permanently and brought Tamil Nadu under direct Madras Presidency rule.
To trace the freedom dawn: tax & tribute resistance (Pulithevar/Kattabomman) -> 1801 unity call (Marudhu) -> 1806 military rising (Vellore).
These fearless pioneers planted the very first seeds of Indian independence on Tamil soil.

board.text: Early Tamil heroes lit the freedom spark

problem.en: Why is the Vellore Revolt of 1806 called a precursor to the Great Revolt of 1857?

text.en: Compare the trigger.

why.en: Like 1857's greased cartridges, Vellore's 1806 Agnew turban order violated both Hindu and Muslim soldiers' religious traditions.

text.en: Compare the unity & symbol.

why.en: Indian sepoys united overnight, seized Vellore Fort and proclaimed a traditional ruler (Tipu's son Futteh Hyder).

text.en: Note the timeline.

why.en: Occurring 51 years before Meerut, Vellore demonstrated how deep resentment among Indian sepoys could ignite an anti-British uprising.
